Such unchanged genitives,in turn,are often avoided and paraphrased:''der Vater von Max'' (colloquially:''vom Max'').}The genitive is formed with -s after ''-ia'':''Claudias,Marias''. Only the form Mariens remains current,but it is restricted to the Virgin Mary.|Suffix}#forms adverbs from superlatives and ordinal numbers}•''der'' erste → erstens}•''am'' meisten → meistens}•''am'' besten → bestens}•''am'' frühesten → frühestens|Usage notes}Adverbs in ''@^'' often have an absolute superlative sense,meaning “at most,maximally” or “very much,exceedingly”. These forms are widely lexicalized,however. That is to say that they cannot be formed freely,except in poetic or humorous language.

Erbfeind*German{}2017|Etymology}<4tthe Devil as the hereditary enemy of mankind. Equivalent to Erbe,(inheritance) heritage,Feind,(enemy).}Since the 15th century used of the Turks (seen as infidel and followers of the Devil). Then generalised to any long-standing enmity without religious context. The new narrowing to the French is an influence of 19th-century nationalism,which resented France for the Napeolonic invasions and for its general opposition to German national unity. This narrowing was never absolute,however,and the word continued to be used in other contexts.é0/ˈɛrpˌfaɪ̯nt/}Ⓓ1/1f/é8)}#A historical enemy,hereditary (inherited) or sworn enemy believed to be hostile for generations male or of unspecified gender}#}Jakob Kubli,"Marke zeigt vereinigtes Korea",''Neue Zürcher Zeitung'',1 February 2016.}#}:Im Disput zwischen Südkorea und Japan hat sich Nordkorea mit seinem '''@^''' Südkorea stets solidarisch erklärt.+In the dispute between South Korea and Japan,North Korea declared solidarity with its '''historical enemy''' South Korea every time.}#dated the Devil}•synononym:[Teufel],[Satan],[Luzifer],[Höllenfürst]|Usage notes}In German historic consciousness the term is mostly associated with the French,and by extension the Romans,as supposed hereditary enemies of the Germans/Germanics. -erweise*{2-er Weise|Etymology}From the genitive feminine singular adjective ending  and the feminine noun Weise. This was originally an adverbial genitive first used in Middle High German. For example,nointerptrue. Adverbs formed this way represent univerbations of genitive absolute adjective-noun phrases.é0/ɐˌvaɪ̯zə/|Suffix}#Used to form adverbs from adjectives and participles; these adverbs are used to modify phrases or sentences. Cognate with English -wise.}•normal}•traurig}•lustig}•gleich|Usage notes}A normal German adverb,which modifies verbs,nouns,adjectives,or (other) adverbs,is identical to the basic form of the respective adjective. Only when an adverb refers to a whole phrase or sentence does it take the ending ''@^''. The distinction may be semantic. Compare:}: (He felt sad as he returned to his homeland.)}: (It is sad that he returned to his homeland.)|Derived terms}suffixsee:de|See also}-weise

es faustdick hinter den Ohren haben*{2es hinter den Ohren haben|Etymology}Literally:[to have it fist-thick behind the ears]. The idiom is rooted in the old popular belief that waggishness and trickiness were little demons that sat behind people’s ears and were recognizable by thick bumps or lumps. -falls*!0Suffixation of the conjunction falls,this presumably from the genitive of Fall.é0/fals/|Suffix}#used to form adverbs from adjectives<ref name"Leo Grammatik"> https://dict.leo.org/grammatik/deutsch/Wortbildungsregeln/Derivation/To-Adv/Suffixe/falls.xml?langen#id2.1.4.6.3</ref>}•gleich}•besten}•notwendig}#used to form adverbs from pronouns<ref name"Leo Grammatik"></ref>}•kein}•ander|Usage notes}This suffix forms adverbs that imply a particular condition or circumstance,similarly to phrases like "in case of," "if," or "in the event of" in English,and it adds a hypothetical or conditional sense to words.}The adverbs are formed either from an adjective or from a pronoun.}Since the suffix comes from a genitive formation,adjectives are often accompanied by an interfix -en,which originally corresponds to the strong masculine singular declension of the adjective itself.}For the same reason,some pronouns could present the interfix -es,as in keinesfalls.|Derived terms}suffixsee:de

falten*£3 valden,£9 valten,`b faldan,`b faltan,é7 ⋆falþan. The irregular forms with ''-t-'' arose through early levelling of Grammatischer Wechsel,but remained rare in both Old and Middle High German. They probably established themselves in modern German by analogy as there are several verbs in ''-alten'' (halten,schalten,spalten,walten),but none in ''-alden''.é0/ˈfaltən/}Ⓓ/a/a0/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Ⓓe/ed/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:altn̩|Verb}@^(faltete,gefaltet:ge@^regional)}#to fold}•seine Hände '''@^'''}•to '''fold''' one's hands}•mit '''gefalteten''' Händen}•with '''folded''' hands|Usage notes}The normal past participle is gefaltet. fangen*£3 vāhen,`b fāhan,a strong verb with past forms `b fieng,`b gefangan,é7 ⋆fą̄han,from Proto-Germanic ⋆fanhaną. The present stem ''fang-'' is derived from the past forms. This development spread ?H vangen to Central German dialects of early modern German (compare already from Old Saxon fangan alongside from Old Saxon fāhan). The same happened in hängen (< ''hāhen''),in which,however,the development was reinforced by the existence of two variant verbs and therefore established itself much faster than it did in ''@^''. (Still today from Alemannic German foo is used in many dialects of Swiss German.) Cognate to from German Low German to catch,from Dutch to catch,from Swedish to get,receive,from West Frisian to catch,from Danish to get,receive,from English to lay hold of,from Albanian to hinder,hold captive.é0/ˈfaŋən/+ˈfaŋən+ˈfaŋŋ̩}Ⓓ3/3c/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ/6/61/De-@^2.ogg(Berlin)(Berlin)}Rhymes:aŋn̩|Verb}@^(fängt#fing,ge@^)}#transitive to catch Literally:[grab something flying in the air]}•Der Torwart '''fängt''' den Ball.}•The goalkeeper '''catches''' the ball.}#transitive to catch; to capture Literally:[to take hold of a person or an animal]}•Die Förster '''fingen''' das entlaufene Wildschwein.}•The rangers '''caught''' the run-away boar.}#reflexive to improve in health; do well again; to do better}•Es sah schlecht um sie aus,aber jetzt hat sie sich wieder '''ge@^.'''}•It looked quite bad for her,but now she has '''improved''' again.}#reflexive to calm down; to compose oneself}•Wenn du dich '''ge@^''' hast,kannst du jetzt essen kommen.}•If you’ve '''composed''' yourself,you may come to dinner now.}#colloquial to catch (a disease; something unpleasant)}•Ich hab mir auf der Kirmes nur ’ne Grippe '''ge@^.'''}•All I '''caught''' at the fun fair was a flu.}#colloquial to be slapped @^ ( with  :eine)}•Sag das noch mal und du '''fängst''' dir eine.}•Say that again and you’ll '''catch''' it.|Derived terms}ab@^}an@^}auf@^}ein@^}emp@^}um@^}unter@^}ver@^
